title: Luzzatto's Path of the Just
hookLine: Moshe Chaim Luzzatto's 1740 ladder of traits
carry: the path of the just begins with the obvious

lines: ONE TRAIT LEADS TO THE NEXT.
cards: A book usually promises something new. This one opens by saying the opposite. Its author tells the reader, in effect: I haven't written this to teach you anything you don't know.

I've written it to remind you of what you already know, and pass over every day. Then, chapter by chapter, he lays out a road, one trait leading to the next. Some Mussar students still study it, with a partner or alone.

teach.b: Mesillat Yesharim. The path of the upright, or the path of the just. Turn it four ways.
First, the author: Rabbi Moshe Chaim Luzzatto, from Italy, known by his initials as the Ramchal.

This path met him earlier; this is his short book on character. Second, the reminder. The introduction says the things in it are well known: everyone agrees that piety, humility and the fear of Heaven matter.
The trouble is that because they're so familiar, nobody stops to study them. People study what's hard and skip what's obvious, so the obvious never gets lived.
His book slows a reader down on exactly those familiar things. Third, the ladder. Luzzatto didn't invent the order.

He took it from a teaching of Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair, kept in the Talmud: Torah leads to watchfulness, watchfulness to zeal, zeal to cleanliness, cleanliness to separation, separation to purity, purity to piety, piety to humility, humility to fear of sin, fear of sin to holiness.
Each rung rests on the one below. You don't leap to holiness. You start by paying attention.
Fourth, why a path. A path isn't a list; it has a first step and a direction.

teach.h: A ROUTE, NOT A PILE OF IDEAS.
teach.b: The traits of recent weeks, truth, trust, generosity, honor, guarded speech, stop being a pile of good ideas here and become a route.
The next days follow it, one rung at a time.

how: Mussar students study Mesillat Yesharim, often a chapter at a time with a study partner or in a group, working through its traits in order from watchfulness toward holiness.

games.q: you're Luzzatto, writing a book on how to become a better person. how do you open it?
o: promise readers secrets they've never heard.
say you're reminding them of what they already know.
start with the highest level, holiness.
games.why: his introduction says the book isn't meant to teach anything new, but to remind readers of what is familiar and so easily skipped.

practice: Picture your character as a road, with you standing somewhere along it, and don't judge where.
Notice one good thing so familiar you've stopped seeing it, calling a parent, keeping a small promise, thanking someone you pass every day, since the obvious is exactly what slips.
See yourself doing it once, on purpose; that's the rung, and if you pray, you can ask for help with the next step.
